candidates.above_next: It reorganizes the entire object model, where the next only governs when a value may be absent.

also.why: a stance that the language should not privilege the implementor's categories over the programmer's

beats.why: general-purpose positioning claims a scope, it does not reshape how you think

harms: erases useful distinctions between values and types
invites misuse by making everything assignable and storable
uniform object overhead even on simple integers
candidates.instead_of: privileged built-ins that can't be passed or stored like ordinary values
candidates.quote: In L, all objects that can be named are said to be "first class."
candidates.statement: Give every nameable thing equal status, assignable, passable and storable, rather than privileging some kinds of object.

strongest.why: equal status for everything nameable dissolves the hierarchy between kinds of thing, so functions, classes and modules become data you manipulate

candidates.above_next: Its charge about correctness strikes harder than the aesthetic pleasure of a round-tripping representation.

also.why: it makes the absence of a correct value a first-class event, an exception, rather than a sentinel to be forgotten

beats.why: sparing users uninteresting details is a comfort rule; demanding that no error pass silently is a safety stance with teeth

harms: forces exception handling even on fast paths
raising on overflow surprised C-trained users
can abort a long computation instead of returning a usable partial
candidates.instead_of: silent sentinels, truncation or undefined behavior as in C
candidates.quote: I decided that there should be no undefined result values in L – instead, exceptions should always be raised when no correct return value can be computed.
candidates.statement: When no correct value can be computed, raise rather than return an undefined or silently clipped result, and reject inconsistent constructions outright.

strongest.why: it refuses the C habit of silent wrong answers; a wrong computation must announce itself

candidates.above_next: Its elegance is real but narrower than the indexing convention that shapes every loop and slice.

also.why: it ties the printed form to the parser, making representation and construction one idea

beats.why: borrowing set-builder notation is a pretty formulation; the repr rule is a general invariant every type must satisfy

harms: not every object has a sensible constructor expression
forces ugly forms like the trailing-comma one-tuple
the guarantee breaks for cyclic or huge structures
candidates.instead_of: arbitrary, unparseable string descriptions of objects
candidates.quote: One of the rules I took from the predecessor was that every data type, when printed or converted to a string, should be represented by an expression that was a valid input to the language's parser.
candidates.statement: Make a value's printed form a valid expression that reconstructs it, rather than a free-form description.

strongest.why: a printed value you can paste back as code is an economical, closed loop between a value and its text

candidates.above_next: A convention every slice obeys spreads wider than how instance variables are named.

also.why: it reframes an index as a position between elements rather than on one

beats.why: preferring comprehensions to map/filter is a taste; the half-open convention is a structural invariant you compute with

harms: half-open intervals confuse beginners expecting inclusive ends
0-based clashes with domains that count from one
off-by-one still bites at the boundaries
candidates.quote: Using / 0-based indexing, half-open intervals, and suitable defaults (as L / ended up having), they are beautiful: a[:n] and a[i:i+n]
candidates.statement: Index from zero with half-open intervals and suitable defaults so adjacent slices meet without off-by-one corrections.

strongest.why: the adjacency invariant, one slice's end is the next's start, removes +1/-1 noise and is simply beautiful

candidates.above_next: Explicitness reorganizes how one writes methods, where the sequence concept, next, unifies how one reads collections.

also.why: a method becomes just a function whose first argument is the object, needing no special method syntax

beats.why: rejecting instance-variable declarations is the negative of the same choice; naming self states the rule positively

harms: every method pays the visual cost of writing self
forgetting self produces confusing errors
explicitness reads verbose next to an implicit this
candidates.instead_of: implicit this and hidden instance-variable lookup as in C++
candidates.quote: With explicit references, there is no need to have a special syntax for method definitions nor do you have to worry about complicated semantics concerning variable lookup. Instead, one simply defines a function whose first argument corresponds to the instance, which by convention is named "self."
candidates.statement: Make the instance an explicit first argument and explicit attribute access the only way to reach its state, rather than implicit resolution.

strongest.why: it insists the instance be named in the open rather than smuggled in by hidden scope rules

candidates.above_next: A unifying abstraction over data edges out the method-level discipline of avoiding new syntax.

also.why: a single set of operations replaces many type-specific ones

beats.why: making every construct an executable statement unifies the grammar; the sequence unifies the things the programmer actually handles daily

harms: one interface onto lists, tuples and strings hides their differences
a string behaving as a sequence of characters surprises
uniformity tempts operations that don't fit a given type
candidates.instead_of: separate, incompatible operations for each container type
candidates.quote: I decided to generalize these to a common concept, the sequence. This generalization made it so certain core operations such as getting the length (len(s)), indexing (s[i]), slicing (s[i:j]), and iteration (for i in s) worked the same on any sequence type.
candidates.statement: Generalize related types under a shared concept so the same core operations work uniformly across them, rather than per-type operations.

strongest.why: one concept, the sequence, lets length, indexing, slicing and iteration mean the same across unrelated types

also.why: the cost of a new construct falls on everyone, so it must be earned before being added

beats.why: allowing any statement in a class body is one instance of keeping syntax simple; the no-new-syntax rule is the general discipline behind many such choices

harms: reusing existing syntax yields awkward forms like dunder names
overloading one construct can hide intent from readers
avoiding syntax sometimes defers a cleaner solution for years
candidates.instead_of: adding dedicated grammar for each new capability
candidates.quote: A major design constraint was that I didn't want to add syntax for methods that differed from the syntax for functions. Refactoring the grammar and the byte code generator to handle such similar cases differently felt like a huge task.
candidates.statement: Prefer the minimal solution that reuses existing syntax over introducing new syntax for a new feature.

strongest.why: solving a new need by reusing what exists, with no new grammar, keeps the language small
